topic: Manipur Gets Elected Government After President's Rule

subtopics.title: New Government in Manipur
subtopics.summary: President Droupadi Murmu revoked President's Rule in Manipur after nearly one year, clearing the path for an elected government. Yumnam Khemchand Singh (BJP) was sworn in as the 13th Manipur Chief Minister. Two Deputy Chief Ministers, Nemcha Kipgen and Losii Dikho, took oath alongside him.
facts: President Droupadi Murmu revoked President's Rule in Manipur

subtopics.title: Kuki-Zomi and Meitei Violence
subtopics.summary: Violence erupted between Kuki-Zomi tribals and the Meitei community, the first clash of its kind in three decades in Manipur. A key trigger was the Meitei demand for Scheduled Tribe (ST) status, which has persisted since 2012. A 2023 High Court direction to consider that request added to tensions with Kuki groups.

subtopics.title: Historical Background and Divides
subtopics.summary: Meiteis make up 52 per cent of Manipur's population and live mainly in valley areas covering about 10 per cent of the state. Hill areas cover 89 per cent of the land but have only 20 of the 60 assembly seats, while Meiteis hold 40. Meiteis are restricted from buying land in about 90 per cent of Manipur, whereas tribals can buy land in the Imphal Valley.

subtopics.title: President's Rule: Articles, Duration and Revocation
subtopics.summary: President's Rule is the Centre's takeover of a state government when the constitutional machinery fails, also called State Emergency. A proclamation must be approved by both Houses of Parliament within 2 months, and then continues for 6 months. It can be extended by Parliament up to a maximum of 3 years and can be revoked by the President at any time.
facts: Article 355 imposes a duty on the Centre to ensure state governments run per the Constitution
Article 356 lets the President act when a state government cannot function per the Constitution
Article 365 covers a state's failure to comply with directions from the Centre

Maximum extension period is 3 years
Resolutions need a simple majority of members present and voting
Proclamation can be revoked by a later proclamation without Parliamentary approval
President can take over state government functions and powers of Governor
President can declare that Parliament will exercise state legislature powers

subtopics.title: Key Records and Judicial Review
subtopics.summary: Manipur has had President's Rule the most number of times, 11, followed by UP, J&K and Punjab. The first three instances were in Punjab, PEPSU and Andhra. In S.R. Bommai vs Union of India (1994), the Supreme Court held that the President's power to dismiss a state government is not absolute.
facts: First three President's Rule: Punjab (1951), PEPSU (1953), Andhra (1954)
Most instances: Manipur (11), UP (10), J&K (9), Punjab (8)
Longest total duration: J&K, then Punjab, then Puducherry
Shortest total duration: Uttarakhand
Longest single period: J&K
Shortest single periods: West Bengal, Bihar, Maharashtra
38th Amendment Act of 1975 made the President's satisfaction final and not challengeable in any court
Beyond 1 year, extension needs a National Emergency in operation and Election Commission certification
S.R. Bommai vs Union of India (1994): power to dismiss a state government is not absolute
Till Parliament approves, President can only suspend the Legislative Assembly

The conflict is set against a long history of differences over land, representation and administration. Meiteis form the largest population group in Manipur, while the hill areas cover most of the state's land. Hill communities have raised their own concerns, and different groups have sought political autonomy or separate administrative units. Court proceedings have also played a part in the sequence of events, as the Manipur High Court dealt with petitions connected to the community's status. The state government took several administrative actions during the period, including steps relating to armed groups and land-related disputes in the hills. Each of these decisions was received differently by the communities concerned, and the events were reported as a serious law and order crisis. The events placed heavy strain on relations between the groups living in the state. The episode also drew comment on the state's wider historical divisions. The disruption affected the daily life of people across the state, and the government faced sustained pressure to restore public confidence. The sequence of events was closely followed in the wider country, and it raised questions about how the state would manage its divided communities in the months ahead.

The state government has also taken actions including evictions linked to forest land, and the suspension of an operations agreement with armed groups was later withdrawn. These events came in a period of growing law and order concern, and the government of the day faced demands to step down. The situation shows how land, status and security concerns have become linked in the state's public life. Several of these developments were reported widely and shaped the debate on how the state should respond to the violence. The episode drew national attention to the state's recent politics.

Census data and the drawing of constituency boundaries have drawn attention from several groups, and the state's external border has added to security concerns in recent years. The state's constitutional history includes several stages of change, and its institutions have developed through those stages. Its landscape is divided between a populous plain and large upland tracts, and this geography shapes how land can be owned and how seats are allotted in the legislature. The combination of these factors has made Manipur's politics complex, with each issue linked to questions of identity, representation and security. quizzes.passage: Indian states have sometimes been placed under direct central control when their elected governments cannot run the administration in line with the Constitution. This arrangement is commonly called by a name that refers to the President, and it sits within a wider framework of constitutional emergency provisions. The history of this arrangement reaches back to the early years after independence, when Punjab, PEPSU and Andhra were among the first units brought under it. The records of the later instances show wide differences in how often and for how long each state remained under it. Over time the power drew sustained attention from the courts, and questions about how far the central government could go in using it became part of legal debate. The Constitution sets out the procedure for placing a state under such control, the approval needed from Parliament, and the period for which the arrangement can run. Manipur is among the states that have experienced this arrangement several times. Its political history is therefore closely tied to the repeated use of this power, and the issue remains a subject of constitutional discussion in the state and at the national level. Each instance is recorded separately, with its own dates and duration. The records are useful for comparing one instance with another.

quizzes.passage: A state's elected government may fail to run its administration in line with the Constitution. When that happens, the Union can take direct control of the state, and the arrangement is widely discussed in India under a name tied to the head of the Union. The power is connected to the Centre's responsibility to see that every state is governed according to the Constitution. Its use has a long record, and the first instances in the country date to the early period after independence. Such records show that the length of each instance has differed from one state to another. The power has also been examined by courts, which have looked at how far the central action can go. Legal debates have addressed the scope of the Centre's power, the steps needed for parliamentary involvement, and the powers that remain with the state legislature during the period. The Constitution sets out the procedure for the arrangement, including how a proclamation is approved and how long it can last. Manipur has experienced this arrangement more than once, which has made the topic a recurring subject in the state's political history. The records of each instance include the dates on which the arrangement began.
